title: Abu Bakr's will
hookLine: dying, he names Umar and leaves almost nothing (reported)

lines: WHAT DAY DID THE PROPHET DIE?
cards: An old man lies ill, and he asks his daughter a strange question. In how many cloths was the Prophet wrapped for burial? Then another: on what day did the Prophet die?
Monday, she says. And what day is it today? Monday again.
He hopes, he says, to die before tonight is out. The daughter is Aisha. The father is Abu Bakr, the khalifah, leader of the whole community, and he is arranging his own departure as simply as he can.

teach.b: Bukhari keeps the scene. The Prophet, Aisha answers, was wrapped in three white cloths. Abu Bakr looks at the garment he has been wearing in his illness, which has a stain of saffron on it.

teach.h: WASH THIS ONE, AND ADD TWO.
teach.b: Wash this one, he says, add two more, and wrap me in them. Aisha protests: but it's worn.

teach.h: THE LIVING HAVE MORE RIGHT TO THE NEW.
teach.b: And he answers: the living have more right to the new than the dead. It is only for what the body gives back to the earth. The leader of the whole community, asking to be buried in a used garment.
The histories add more, and they are clear that these are reports. Tradition says Abu Bakr asked that whatever his household had gained while he held office be handed on to the next leader.
When it arrived, the reports describe very little: an animal, a servant, a worn cloth.

teach.h: YOU HAVE MADE IT HARD FOR WHOEVER COMES NEXT.
teach.b: And they say Umar wept and said, you have made it hard for whoever comes after you. Before he died, the histories also say, Abu Bakr consulted some of the companions and then had it written that Umar would lead after him.

Sunni Muslims see this as a rightful choice made by a rightful caliph. Shia Muslims, as earlier days described, see the whole succession differently. The reports themselves describe a man who did not get rich from power.
And he was buried in Aisha's room, beside the friend he had followed.
So the succession story that began with the day after ends here: a pledge, a speech, a hard season, and a man who left almost nothing. Tomorrow a new part begins, with Umar.

how: Muslims retell Abu Bakr's deathbed request for a washed, worn garment as a lesson in simplicity; his grave lies beside the Prophet's in the mosque at Medina.

o: the leader who chose year one of the calendar
the Prophet's son-in-law, married to his daughter Fatimah
the Prophet's friend, who left office owning almost nothing

games.q: Abu Bakr's will — tap the pairs.
p: wash it and add two more
to the new than the dead

s: Abu Bakr asked to be wrapped in new cloth like the Prophet
he asked for his own worn garment, washed, with two more added: the living have more right to the new.
Abu Bakr asked Aisha what day the Prophet had died
Bukhari records the question; she said Monday.
the reports say Umar praised the large estate he received
they describe very little, and say Umar wept: you have made it hard for whoever comes after you.

games.q: you're Aisha. your father, the leader of the community, wants to be buried in his own stained garment. what do you say?
o: nothing. you do exactly as he asks.
games.why: she said it was worn. he answered: the living have more right to the new than the dead.

practice: Bring to mind the things you own that you never use: a drawer, a closet, a shelf. Choose one, a coat, a tool, a book, that someone living needs more than you do, and picture where it could go. The living have more right to the new.

wordCard.voice: Abu Bakr, who asked to be buried in a worn, washed garment, gave back what his office had gained, and named Umar to lead after him. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a will or final instruction, the word used for what a dying person asks.

carryVoice: Your line: he left almost nothing. A worn garment, washed, was enough for him. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1387 (Abu Bakr asks Aisha about the day and the shroud; 'the living have more right to the new')
Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Funerals, chapter on the graves of the Prophet, Abu Bakr and Umar (c. 1390–1392) (burial in Aisha's room beside the Prophet)
Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; al-Tabari, Tarikh (gains in office returned; Umar's weeping; Umar named)
